prompt: In many countries, companies are employing fewer permanent staff and are using more short-term contractors and gig workers. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
Nothing about this change alters how much work needs doing, how uncertain demand is, or how often people fall ill. What it alters is who absorbs those facts. Read that way, the development is a negative one, and the flexibility it is usually defended with turns out to be a description of what happens to whoever is now holding the risk.

Employment law developed as a way of pooling ordinary uncertainty. A firm with two hundred salaried staff can carry a quiet quarter, a flu outbreak and a family emergency without any individual bearing the whole weight of them, because it is large enough to average across them. Convert those staff into contractors and the uncertainty does not disappear; it is divided into two hundred pieces and handed to the people least able to smooth it. A slow week that a company would barely notice becomes a missed rent payment for a driver.

For a minority the trade is worth taking. Specialists whose skills are scarce can price the risk they are absorbing and often come out ahead, and for people whose lives cannot accommodate fixed hours, irregular work is better than no work. But scarcity is what makes that bargain function, and most of the jobs being reclassified are jobs in which the worker is easily replaced. Without bargaining power, flexibility runs in one direction only: the platform varies the hours and the worker accepts them.

The remedy is not to abolish short-term work, which genuinely suits some people and some industries. It is to stop letting the contract label determine the protections, so that sick pay and notice attach to the work rather than to a category. Until that happens, this remains a transfer of risk from balance sheets that can carry it to households that cannot, which is a bad development however much freedom it is described as offering.
title: Permanent jobs giving way to gig and contract work
